BRITISH TROOPS I IN THE COLONIES. A return has just been laid before Parliament which, in connexion with a recent resolution of Government, suggests some curious reflections. It exhibits the numbers and composition of the. several garrisons employed in the protection of British dependencies in every quarter of the globe. The immediate design of the paper was to present a view of the charges thus entailed by each Colony on the Imperial Exchequer, and the information so communicated has, unquestionably, its own points of interest. We prefer, however, on this occasion, to indicate another feature of the case. It ever the famous come, and the stoy of an extinct day of the N> w Z alander should Itritish really empire be reviewed for the instruction of an Australian world, the magnitude of our possessions will not excite more astonishment than the smallness of the force by wliieli they were retained. Dominions on which the sun never sets are held by fewer troops than are probably now assembled at Washington to protect the capital of the Union against its own citizens. It is almost ludicrous to compare the strength of our garrisons with the extent of our territories. Even our purely military settlements are very slenderly furnished. There are not so many soldiers in Malta and Gibraltar together, as would be quartered in a third-rate fortress in any continental kingdom. We ought to premise that t|ie return is made for the year ending March 31, IS59 ; but that was a fair period for taking tin estimate. It was

on New Year's Day in that year that the first note of European war was sounded, and, though there have been displacements of troops since that time, the aggregate strength of our colonial garrisons has probably not been much affected. So we put the figures before the reader, and beg him to mark with how few troops an empire may be governed. The first dependency on the list, and that with which our observations are most directly concerned, is British America. Half the American Continent pertains to the British Crown; and this dependency, so vast and valuable, lies on the borders of a powerful and aggressive Republic. The people of the United States have often amused themselves with talk about the appropriati on of Canada, and have elevated into a "doctrine" the theory that the whole continent is theirs, and that, though foreign claims may be allowed to die out, they must never receive any fresh confirmation or extension. Under such circumstances, it might lie fancied that onr border would be bristling with bayonets, and that a colony so healthy as well as so immense would absorb an army of Itself. Very different is the truth ot the case. The entire garrison of Canada might be packed in a couple of steamers. A good half of all the troops quartered ip the province might he comfortably accommodated in the Wellington Barracks. There are some 20(10 in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, but if every soldier was taken from every North American station, and the whole force
was paraded in a mass, it would barely exceed 5000 men. Que of these stations is Newfoundland. The last mails have informed us that even Newfoundland has

& &H) G its liabilities to political disturbances. Election riots have taken place there, and "ilic troops" have been called out, as in former days they used to beat home. What was the muster of the garrison in the hour of need we do not know, but in March, 1861, it consisted, for all the districts of the Island, ot 199 foot soldiers and one gunner. How this artilleryman came to be so isolated, or what description of piece he was expected to manage, we cannot pretend to guess; but we have to announce that, in consequence of events which have convulsed the American Republic, and arrayed Hie millions ot the North against 1 1t i millions of the South, it lias been determii ed to reinforce the garrison of Canada with a brigade of British Infantry. 100,000 troops of the Royal Army may be considered us employed on foreign service. No cavalry force is engaged in this duty- except in India, which takes about 5000 men from that branch of of the army, and leaves twice that number at home. Of the artillery rather more than 5000 are in India, and somewhat fewer than 4000 in t he colonies leaving 5000 at home. The engineers are more capriciously distributed. India has none, the colonies take about lis garrisons, however, j 1200, and some 3300 are left at home ; hut it is in the colonial stations that the chief contrasts are to be found. That there should he engineers at Gibraltar, at Malta, and at Bermuda is natural enough, and it is equally natural, wc suppose, that tl e Cape should put in its claim for this as for every other species of supply. But it is carious that Western Australia, which is contented with 95 infantry, should want 75 engineers, while all the rest of Australia has hut 26, and Canada only eight. In Nova Scotia, however, and New Brunswick there is a considerable muster of this scientific force, but there are only 11 engineers in all the West Indies, and only 9 in Ceylon. We have heard something lately at out fortifications at St. Helena, and, if there was any work of this kind to he done, it was cestainly wise to send some engineers out, for there were but a couple of these soldiers there in 1859. However, to bring our whole survey to a focus, we may say that of a total present force of about 145000 men of all arms and ranks, we

send 34,000 infantry, 3,800 artillery, and 1 ,200 engineers for service in the several dependencies of the Empire. To the Editor of the St Croix Avis, Sir ! Please insert in your piper the following extract from the Easy Chair of Harper's Magazine for August. The Italics are mine. Your obdt. Servt , X. "The oilier day person a who will read this sent an anonymous letter to the Easy Chair. Of course, dear Sir, you can not understand the profound meanness of such a thing. If you could you wou'd not have done it. It was only a spirt of spite ; shrug a of imbecile enmity. What else can an anonymous letter be ? Show me a man who will insult a woman if he thinks no other man is near, and I will show you a man who piobably writes anonymous letters. For, suppose that you think auotber man wrong, do you not see that if you think so strongly enough to speak about it at all, you ought to speak to him upon your own responsibility r For instance, let us suppose that Mr. Easy Chair has anuoyed Mr. Lambkin by something that be lias said about Garibaldi. Mr. Lambkin is of opinion, let us say, that Garibaldi is a drunken ape and mowiug idiot. When, therefore, lie reads that Mr. Ea>y Chair thinks him a hero Lambkin is wroth. Now, if he speaks to Easy Chair about the matter, and says that lie thinks him for this reason and the other reason to be wrong, Easy Chair listens, and knows, at least, that Lambkin has an honest opinion which may seem to be very erroneous, but is yet something of which Lambkin is not ashamed. If, however, Mr. Lambkin sends an anonymous uote iustead, Mr. Easy Chair smiles because he knows that here is

somebody who does not dare to confess his own opinion, and that cowardice prevents the opinion from even seeming reasonable. The instiiiet of all decent men is, What can be so contempti- 1 ble as the opinion of auy man who is capable of writing an anonymous letter?' But an anonymous letter, you think, may bu an alarming threat. Yes, it may be a threat. And you think that it may be executed? Yes, again; for every man is at the tnerey of a coward. And the danger which is menaced by an anonymous letter no foresight can avoid. The menace is the certificate of treachery. See, also, what a confession it is. Why does not Lambkin sign his name to his letter? Because he knows that the name would give no weight to it , or because he is afraid that the name would be exposed, or because he is afraid that the recipient in the language of the rude street boy, would ' take the change out of his hided , "

From the London Times, August 14. Every Englishman knows, by the experience of his own country, where the shoe would begin to pinch the American belligerents. In that country, as elstvhere, any nun, her of men can be

procured to fight, after some fashion, in any cause, good or had, if they are only well paid, well fed, well clothed, well housed, and moderately well commanded, with some prospect, if not of booty, at least of a whole skin. So i becomes a question of money. A confidence in money alone has always proved false ; hut money there must he, and there is no country in which it is more necessary than in the United States, where wages are high and work is abundant. A war will cost there almost as much as it did here, for if the work is nearer home, and the area of the war somewhat less than the whole surface of this terraqueous globe, still, for that very reason, there is much interruption of the ordinary pursuits of life. In the first place, all the bonds of debtor and creditor, whether public or private, and all the relations of business in cotton and other cultivation, are at an end. The State Governments themselves set the example of repudiation by refusing to cash bonds, or coupons, which can he traced to the possession of the other party in the struggle. Searching interrogatories are put, and must he answered on oath, before a State will pay interest which may find its way to hostile hands. Meanwhile commerce is interrupted by blockades and privateers, and immense works commenced in the depth of peace are stopped by the withdrawal of hands and resources, and not less by a general diminution of confidence in the prospects of the country. At Washington, Finance observes the old forms

of Union, and supposes a tax to he levied on all the States. It is obliged, however, to condescend to fact, and calculate on the certainty that only halt the States will respond" to the call. As is usual in such novel situations, the Federal cause has fed its Treasury from hand to mouth, by such expedients as the issue of Bonds redeemable in GO days, and, of course, to he replaced by similar issues. But the war is now assuming more gigantic proportions ; a hundred thousand men posted in and about Washington are found insufficient and the best excuse that can be made for a disgraceful rout is that many of the States Militia were glad to avail themselves of the expiration of their three months' engagement, and that the enemy had the command of larger reserves. All this shows that, great as the elforts are which have already been made, they are. not up to the mark. Sixty or eighty thousand more men arc demanded, and will soon be in the field. All the Arsenals, Dockyards, and Manufactories of Arms are at work. Immense orders arc despatched to this side the Atlantic, and will he promptly met. All this reminds Englishmen ol the days when war, never too well supplied, cost us sixty or seventy millions sterling a-year. sometimes with no other result than defeat, and loud complaints of insufficient men, money, and munitions. So the Congress of Washington is looking " square in difficulty, the the face;" not so "square," as they say there, however, as they will one day have to

look it. There appears to he no difficulty in- the authorization ol loans to any amount ; indeed, at this moment Government lias large powers for the issue of Treasury notes for three years, and has found the market, we presume, unfavourable for the exercise of its powers. The real question is how to find a proper basis for loans in an augmented and well-paid revenue. This involves taxation, and, unfortunately,

taxation appears to be a point on which the Eastern and Western States of the Federal Union are almost as much at variance as both are with the Southern Confederacy. The Western States have a particular objection to taxes ; and when we read the War Budget which the Congress seems finally to have decided on one feels that such an objection may be expressed not only in good sentences on the floor of Congress, but also in a not less formidable manner Far West. Besides a direct tax of 20,000,01)0 dollars apportioned among the States, and expected from only half, the new Budget proposes a tax upon carriages, varying from one dollar to fifty 5 a tax upon watches; an Excise duty on spirituous liquors of five cents a-gallon, and on fermented liquors of 60 cents a-barrel ; and a general tax upon Incomes, the rate of which, as well as the Incomes liable, is not yet decided. Meanwhile the Morrill Tariffis untouched except by the imposition of additional duties. Every item in this Budget suggests a financial war, as difficult, if not so sanguinary, as the war in the open field. Our own great war was a period of smuggling by sea and by land. An army of Excisemen, a fleet of Revenue (Titters, and a Coastguard that nightly watched and paced the whole of our shores, were necessary to protect the revenue, without which the war must have come to an end. It cannot be otherwise in the Northern States; of the Southern we speak not, but we shall soon hear the same story there. The United States contain the same

social elements as those which in this country have ever evaded taxation when it was possible. The morality of the taxpayer soon relaxes when his political feelings conspire with his pecuniary interests and his conscience throbs in bis pocket. Already we are told that the Western Slates have certain plausible objections to taxes ; and a majority of the Bankers at Netv York are altogether averse to the war and its causes. All the private intelligence that reaches us agrees in describing that war as the result of mob passions, and the real act of men who have comparatively little interest in the maintenance of union, order, national credit, or property itself. When such is the case they who have incomes, who spend, and who employ will feel small enthusiasm for the war ; as, on the other hand, they who enter into it heart and soul will be generally men of less means, lower social position, and þÿ need we add ? þÿ a laxer tone of morality. What sort of a prospect is this for a succession of War Budgets, like ours from 1793 to 1815, each more colossal, more exhaustive, more ruinous than the last? Washington has already learnt the secret of some of our own military reverses ; it will now learn to sympathize with our war finance. But there is another question which presents itself to the capitalist before even the solvency of a State, or the yield of a tax, or the final success of a cause; and that is the number and frequency of similar calls. If we are to judge from the immense figures on pa-

per paraded by the Northerners, this is a war that may take rank with any of ours, þÿ with the European war, which cost us from first to last more than a thousand millions of money, or the Russian War, which cost us a hundred millions in two years. If the Government of Washington is obliged to ask for a hundred million dollars to-day, when and how soon will it have to re-

ST fV 0 I X A V I peat that demand; and how many such demands will it have to make this year, and for how many years? Every such demand will compete in the market with the Bonds of the last, and our old folks can remember with what celerity a promise to pay 5 1, a-year became worth not so much as 50/. Prudent people do not like buying stock at its present price when they know that twenty or thirty millions more will soon be thrown 011 the market for what it will fetch. Nor is this the only apprehension to damp the courage of the lender. Already, while tl.is war is still in its very cradle, the Bankers of the seaboard States are suggesting, in the form of Treasury Bonds, a very large increase of the paper currency. How long would this be convertible? We may safely predict that if the war lasts as long as it now threatens to last, both sides will be driven to the same pitiable expedient of a depreciated paper currency as the mother country was in a similar extremity. They have an encouragement which we had not; a source of credit which we had not. They know what we never knew, þÿ that we could survive the process and pay our creditors in full. In our history their financiers possess both a warning and an encouragement ; for, if they see the Slough of Despoil.', they see also how Christian got out of it, and scrambled safe up the bank on the other side. These are commercial considerations the soundness of which it is impossible to question, and which address themselves naturally to the Fede-

ral and Confederate Governments, their Congresses, their financiers, and the public, whether Americans or Europeans, who are solicited to lend money for the war. They are, of course, exclusive of political or partisan feelings. No doubt, there are enthusiasts in the United States who will lend money and buy Treasury bonds for three or ten years, all the more freely because they feel deeply the social and religious aspects of the quarrel. There may, too, for aught we know, be abolitionists and philanthropists in this country who will buy American notes in a falling market, and prefer to give a good price for them rather than a bad one, because they care more for the credit of the Federal cause than they do for the amount of their own fortune. We cannot think, however, there are so many such people as largely to affect the quotation of American Securities in our market. England was almost unanimous in its zeal against the disturbers of European order and in lependence. No war ever assumed so sacred and patriotic a character. Indeed, had St. Paul's been the Holy Sepulchre itself', we could not have made more a religion of it. This did not prevent our Public Securities of all kinds from finding their market level, and that a very low one. The whole story will be repeated in the States, --tliat is, unless tbey patch up their differences before long, which they don't seem likely to do. þÿ Important intelligence comes from Hayti by way of Jamaica. The Guardian of the 24th July gives the following

particulars on the authority of a Haytian gentleman in that city: þÿ It appears that about midday on Saturday, the 6th inst., six Spanish war steamers were seen making their way into the harbour of Port-au-Prince. As the news spread through the city it created the greatest excitement, no one

knowing what was the misssion of these vessels. Uncertainty was, however, soon set at rest, for upon the squadron anchoring in the harbour a boat was despatched from the Admiral's ship, conveying an officer who was the bearer of certain papers to General Geffrnrd ; and it shortly transpired that the unexpected visit was to demand satisfaction from the llaytian Government for certain outrages alleged to have been committed upon the frontier of Santo Domingo by Haytien subjects and Dominican exiles resident in the llaytian territory. Those outrages were said to be the pulling down of the Spanish flag and trampling it under foot, and the destruction by fire of the property of the Dominicans. The reparation deþÿ manded by the Spaniards was twofold: first, that the llaytian Government should pay 8200,009 to the Dominican Government ; and second, that the flaytians should salute the Spanish flag with a salute of 100 guns. 48 hours were given to consider these terms; and if at the expiration of that time they were not accepted, the squadron would bombard the town of Port-au-Prince. As may be imagined, these tidings spreading like wildfire through the city caused the greatest consternation ; and, fearing the worst, families began at once to pack up their moveables, and to make other arrangements for leaving the city. Before the time expired, however, the Spanish Admiral, Rivalcaba, was visited by Mr. Ilenry Byron, Her Britannic Majesty's Consul in Hayti, who proposed

a modification of the terms. This was at first refused ; but Mr. Byron urged his proposals with such effect, that it was ultimately agreed upon that, instead of insisting upon the immediate payment of the indemnity, certain parties should be appointed on each side to estimate the damages which had been done ; and, second, that the Spannish flag should be saluted by the Haytian Government. On these conditions the Admiral consented to spare the city the bombardment. President Geffrard's consent was, however, yet to be obtained ; and, although but little difficulty was experienced in getting him to agree to the first condition, it was found no easy task to induce him to comply with the second. Through the remonstrances and solicitations of the different Consuls, he at length consented to salute the Spanish flag, in order to save the city the horrors that were impending over it, giving the command for the salute with tears in his eye, and recording bis solemn protest against an act which nothing, he declared, but the force of utterly uncontrollable circumstances would have ever induced him to sanction. The salute was then fired, after which the llaytian flag was saluted by the squadron. This ended, the Admiral and his principal officers landed, and paid a visit to the President, to whom the Admiral expressed his satisfaction at the peaceful issue of the affair. President Geffrard returned the compliment by sending a few of his aides-de-camps on board the Admiral's

ship, where they were well received. The fleet was to leave Port-au-prince on the 15th inst. " The conduct of Mr. Byron, the British Consul, is spoken of in the highest terms, and had raised him greatly in the estimation of the Havtians. The United

States Consul, too, showed great spirit and determination, strenuously protesting against t lie bombardment, lie raised bis flag, and made known his resolution not to leave hisjiouse, giving the Spaniards warning that should anything happen to him, or any American citizens, his Government would hold theirs responsible for such injury. Happily, the affair came to a pacific solution. The whole thing is, however, eminently the question, says þÿ suggestive of coming events." The Jamaica Tribune , in its remarks on .- "The Haytian journals expected much from their allies from the other side of the Atlantic. VVe hope they may not be doomed to disappointment, but the prospect of foreign aid is exceedingly remote. Not a few persons begin to fear that Louis Napoleon may see fit to make an effort to recover the. western part of the island to France, as Spain has recovered possession of Dominica. At the moment when 1 lay t i is thus threatened with invasion there has also been a revival of the unhappy disputes between the blacks and the mulatto l be latter favouring a French protecto- population, rate as likely to give them a greater proportion of the offices. The blacks are loyal. Trouble has also been experienced with the free people of color who migrated from America. It is charged that they were allowed only $3 per day Haytian currency, which is equal to 115 cent, of ours, wherewith to support their families. The prospect of maintaining Haytinn independence, except at

a frightful sacrifice of life, was gloomy." Garibaldi on tiik Nationalities. þÿ Garibaldi has addressed the following letter to the Countess d'Ora d'lstris, nee Princess Ghika " Caprera, July þÿ16, Madame, I have read with admiration and gratitude your charming letter. It strengthens in me the opinion I have long entertained that woman is called by Providence to play the first part in the emancipation of oppressed nationalities and in the annihilation of despotism. You arc right, Madame : the Papacy is the most horrible plague that my poor country . is afflicted with : eighteen centuries of false hood, persecution, and burning at the stake, complicity with all the tyrants of in Italy, rendered the plague incurable. At present, as heretofore, this vampire of the land of the Scipios supports its body, which is corrupted and eaten up by gangrene, by means of discord, reaction, pillage. and civil war; and it affords a pretext for keeping permanently in Italy a foreign army, which by its influence prevents a generous nation from constituting itself. Hungary is at the present moment in a very delicate situation. The Hungarian people, who on the field of Italian liberty have cemented their fraternal alliance with us, well deserve the co operation of the nations of Eastern Europe, whose cause is identical with theirs. The Servians, Croats, and Dalmatians have adhered to the national aspiration of the Magyars. The Moldo-Wallacliians ought to imitate that example, and I entertain the full conviction that you will exercise your high

influence over your countrymen to draw closer the paternal ties which ought henceforth to unite the Eastern races with the sister races of the centre and west of Europe. When nations shall love each other and be in accord, as required by the laws of Christ and of humanity, they will realise the dreams of happiness in which I have indulged at all the epochs of life. þÿ G. Garibaldi.

From the St. Thomas Times, September 7. Our issue of last Saturday announced that His Excellency Governor Birch, K. I)., had arrived here from St. Croix, and we have now to mention his departure yesterday morning for St. John's. If we may judge hy 1 1 is Excellency's movements whilst here, we may conclude that he came on an official visit. We therefore hope that the many subjects that have so long been requiring dilinite action will have received their full share of the Governor's attention, and in as far as his prerogative extends, will not he allowed any further useless delay. The condition of our harbour stands prominent of all others. Speaking on the matter, we heard it said, a few days since, on the occasion of the Governor's coming, that the harbour had so often been spoken of, and nothing done, that a very general opinion prevailed, that for another generation it would remain so, unless it happened that one of the British Atlantic steamships should ground, and then the howl that would extend from Dcmerartf to Jamaica would soon serve to kill all circumlocution that has attended it, and at last invoke the good offices of Madame Maricsalope whose capacity for drudging or dredging is very well known. Next, or equal in importance, is the further deepening and widening the

channel at the haul-overs, þÿ a work very well commenced but too abruptly suspended. As far as it has already gone, we hear it remarked hy those residing at the lower end of the harbour, that a marked improvement is seen in the colour of the water, as well as there is apparently a higher tide thereabout, and judging thereby, if the work was executed to the extent fust meditated, the benefits would naturally be more. Then we have the notorious "crablands," of which it may sound " like fic- tion to talk of converting into parks" with "gardens" and charming "bowers," &c. &c., hut in plain practical truth are very susceptible of improvement, and the only thing to us a'-out them appearing like fiction, is the fabulous amount of money it is said will be required to change their present condition. The three sewers, in the three valleys of the town, that empt info the sea the waters that collect from the hills during heavy rains, and of which Mr. M. M. Monsanto, jun., Civil Engineer, lias just completed three superb drawings, shewing their courses, grades and lengths, and the works required for their proper condition, are subjects equally worthy the attention of the Executive ; and as these are attached to the Communal branch of the Administration, we arc of opinion there should be no delay. Any one who would patient Iv walk through those sewers, and for the time endure their fragrance, would hardly fail to notice how property situated on their either side must always

have had a depreciated value, owing to their long unfinished state. Prindsesse Street, and her thirteen sisters in affliction, no. doubt have received the charitable countenance of Mis Excellency; and if he has seen them all, as others do, there is now hope for those doing penance in their neighbourhood, with corns and bunions, to have a speedy reprieve. The proposal too that has recently emanated from the Honorable Burgher Councii, to erect suitable public buildings for the use of our Courts of Law, þÿ the Police Departments, Burgher Council Chambers, »fcc. &.c , þÿ and of which \ wc believe plans have also been made, is a matter no less deserving ot attention. There was a talk in the Colonial Council of St. Croix, this year, of selecting a quarantine station here, and erecting the necessary buildings thereon, but as we have reached the month of September and see no visible sign of it, may he other opinions have since prevailed. In the foregoing we have endeavoured to point out much of the material wants of the place, not even alluding to the project of Gas, which some time hack had lighted up the public mind, but for the present seems again to be put out. Nor have we said anything in reference to the desirability of a Fish-market, and the wish manifested hy a portion of the community with regard to obtaining a suitable site for the proposed Theatre. Then the Government has proposed to subsidise a steamer to run between the two Islands. In regard to this subsidy

we will only say that it may be useful for those who have to deal with the question to remember that one-stiverand-a-half in the colonies has about the par value of a skiiling in Europe. Turning front these topics and contemplating the changes that are likely to arise hy instituting a separate Colonial Council for this Island, and His Excellency's own recent announcement that a Press Law, similar to that existing in Denmark, would be introduced for these

. . I Islands before t he present year expires, we should not wonder if Ilis Excellency has felt some desire to learn the sentiments of the more influential class of this community upon those subjects. It is possible that of this we shall learn very little ; but this we may venture to say, that the information gathered will much depend upon the amount of candour exercised by those to whom the subjects may have been addressed, for some men estimate reserve as a quality of great price. þÿ þÿ United Stale3 Frigate "Pcwhatten"

IMMIGRATION. You will at once perceive that it is desirable that the several colonies should concur in the arrangements which it will be necessary to carry out. These arrangements must be effected by the Land and Emigration Commissioners, who are desirous of ascertaining the wishes of the respective colonial governments on the subject. It strikes me that the minor colonies would in all probability much prefer the establishment of a distinct agency for themselves. It is evident from the public discussions in British Guiana, that the emigration agent for that colony has been unable to satisfy its demands for emigrants, and I have no doubt that there would be a strong objection to his undertaking to supply other coldnies. If the minor colonies should concur in having a separate agent, the question would have to be determined whether it would be more expedient to follow the plan adopted by the colonies of British Guiana and Trinidad, or to employ a mercantile firm as suggested by the West India Committee. My impression is that the colonics of St. Vincent, Grenada, St. Lucia, and St. Kills would be able to take each two shiploads of emigrants annually; and if the cargoes be estimated at 275 each, 2,200 emigrants would be annually required ; the agent's commission on which, at 7 rupees each, would be £1,540, or more than the highest rate paid to separate agents. It is far from improbable that Antigua and Tobago may be added to the list of colonies requiring immigrants, but, no without in- cluding them, there is probability

that the four colonies already mentioned would in any year be unable to receive one cargo each, which would be above 1,000 in the aggregate. The proposition of Messrs. Lyall, Rennie &. Co. would therefore involve a certain payment of £1,000 a-year, which is the salary of the Jamaica agent, and the probable payment of to a higher other ration than is given any remune- emigration agent in Calcutta. I must own that my opinion is that a fixed salary to the agent would be the most desirable arrangement. It is not the interest of the colouies to have vessels filled up with emigrants unfitted for labour ; and I should fear that the tendency of an allowance per capita would be to increase numbers without reference to other considerations. It is far from improbable that Messrs. Lyall, Rennie, &

Co. would be willing to accept a fixed salary of £1,200 a-year, which would be equal to their own proposed commission on 1,500 emigrants, with an understanding that it should be increased to £1,500, if two other colonies should be added to the list. I am, however, inclined to think that the best plan would be to acquaint the Emigration Commissioners, that Messrs. Lyall, Rennie, Co. having been recommended by the West India Committee, would be the most desirable agent for minor colonies, and that it is the wish of those colonies that the Emigration Commissioners should secure their services on the best terms possible. It will be for each colonial government to state whether it gives the preference to a fixed salary or to allowance per capita. 1 may observe that, even if a fixed salary were paid to the agents in Calcutta, the Several colonies might share that salary among themselves in proportion to the nnmber of cargoes shipped to each. The preceding remarks are based on the assumption that Calcutta is the best place to establish an emigration agency for the minor colonies. My belief is that on the whole a Chinese agency would be preferable, although the first cost would doubtless be greater. A second agency would probably be too expensive, and it would, therefore, be desirable to consider whether the preference should be given either to India or China as a field tor the supply of labour to the minor colonies. þÿ Governor llinc/c's Despatch.

A degree of excitement altogether unprecedented was occasioned by the arrival of the "Confederate States" war steamer Sumter on the 30th ult. Everybody fell into a state of perplexity, among the American merchants þÿ alarm, would perhaps be the more correct word. None could tell whether some one of the eleven prizes the Sumter was reported to have captured might not be a vessel from or to this port. Indeed it was stated that the Captain of one of Messrs. A Campbell & Co.'s vessels that left here some time ago had been seen on board. There were vessels bearing the flag of the United States in the Gulf, and others expected, the fate of which, if the Sumter thought proper to wait upon them outside the Bocas, could not be doubtful. Anxiety was felt about one of Messrs. Dwight's vessels, which it was said left here with a considerable amount of specie on 4th instant, and even there seemed to be some fears of the Sea Eagle, now unloading a valuable cargo, consigned to Messrs. C. L. Haley &. Co. The local authorities scarcely knew how to receive officers sailing under this novel flag, for though the British Government have recognized the existence of two belligerent powers in the States, still as far as we know, there has been as yet no recognition of the Confederate States as a sovereign power. We believe that his Excellency declined to receive the officer sent or» shore from the Sumter except as a pri-

vate gentleman, and the same course has been pursued by 11. B. M. Corvette Cadmus, which arrived on Sunday. The Sumter came in here for coals. The opinion of the law officers of the crown having been taken, to the effect that these did not fall within the cate-

gory of prohibited goods the steamer þÿ got" supplied. The officers and men have frequently been on shore, and numerous visits have been paid or. board ! ihe Sumter by gentlemen of t lie town, and by them the courtesy and frank kindness of the officers is spoken of very þÿhighly. Gazette, August 7. þÿ Count Cavour's Estimate of Napoi, f.on iii --Of the character and policy of Louis Napoleon he was accustomed to speak with much freedom. No one had better opportunities than Cavour of sounding their depths. He was the only living man who had ventured to grapple with him face to face, and who used him for his purpose. The estimate he had formed of his capacity was not a high one ; but he fully admitted his fertility of resource, his physical and moral courage, and his knowledge of the people he governs. " lie has no definite policy," he remarked to an English friend. " He has a number of political ideas floating in the mind, none of them matured. They would seem to be convictions founded upon instinct. He will not steadily pursue any single idea if a serious object presents itself, but will give way and take up another. This is the mot de Venigme to his policy- It is by steadily keeping this in view that 1 have succeeded in thwarting his designs, or in inducing him to adopt a measure. The only principle þÿ if principle it can be called þÿ which connects together these various ideas is the establishment of his dynasty, and the conviction that the best way to secure it is

by feeding the national vanity of the French people. He found France, after the fall of the Orleanist and Republican Governments, holding but a second place among the great Powers ; he has raised her to the very first. Look at his wars, look at his foreign policy ; lie has never gone one step beyond what was absolutely necessary to obtain this one object. The principle ostentatiously put forward in the first instance has been forgotten or discarded as soon as his immediate end has been accomplished. It was so in the war with Russia; it has been so in the war with Austria. In the Crimea lie was satisfied with the success of his army in the capture of Sebastopol, which took from the English troops the glory they had earned by their devotion and courage, and to which they would have added had the war continued. In the struggle with Austria he was astounded by the greatness of the victories of Magenta and Solferino. The military glory of France had been satiated, and he thought no more of the liberty of Italy, of that free and united nation which he was to have called into existence from the Alps to the Adriatic. It is this uncertain policy, guided by dynastic and selfish considerations, which makes him so dangerous to you, and which renders it necessary that you should ever be on your guard. Not that he is hostile to England or that he has any definite design against her. On the contrary, he has much affection for your country. He is a man of generous impulses, and has strong feelings of

gratitude towards those who have served and befriended him. At the bottom of his heart he is greatly attached to Italy. His earliest recollections are bound up with her. He is to this day a carbonaro in his desire for Italian freedom and hatred for Austria. He has not forgotten the kindness and hospitality shown to him when an exile in England. He admires your institutions and the charac-

S T. C R 0 (1 X A VIS.. ter of the English people. But all this is nothing when compared with the j maintenance of his dynasty, the cstab- | I ishment of which he looks upon almost j in the light of a religious obligation. If the moment came when he thought a sacrifice necessary to sustain it, however great that sacrifice might he, however painful or repugnant to his feelings, he would make it. Np one has had better opportunities of knowing him than I have. He has talked to me with the greatest openness of his future plans. But he has invariably assured me at the same time that his first object was to maintain peace and good understanding with England. "1 believe," he solemnly added, "that, from policy, as well as from affection, such are his views; and that only in a moment of the utmost emergency, when he was convinced that his influence iti France depended upon it, would he depart from them. But that moment may come, and you would be madmen if you were not prepared for it." þÿ Quarterly Review.

There is a good deal said and written about. Austrian and Russian tendencies, and we all know what grievances such sayings hint at, hut ours is even a more aggravated case, lor, if the Venetians are not Austrians or the Doles not Russians, we are Danes, we have not any other nationality. table natives, filling all their lives subordinate situations in the public offices, clcik-hips tn our hanks and stores, to whom controller situations with a $1000 or $12u0 salary p. a., would he a gtteat boon; the more so if they could entertain the slightest hope, in caseol vacancy, of becoming superintend lit of customs with n salaty of $1800, instead of the 2400 now attached to that office. We think the customs depiiitment is one particularly well adapted lor the forwarding of natives us u does not call lor any high judicial acquirements. Is it not then preposterous, that we should be called on to increase the controllers' salaries, just in order that nol -natives, be tuduced to seek these situations ? Although His Excellency has unfortunately fathered the prineiph s above pointed out, we are inclined to think they ate the promptings ol a suhotdmate, and we most re.-pcetiuily hope that His Excellency will give the remark we here submit, his enlightened consideiation. We venture to entertain this hope the more readily, wheu we glance at the futility of the argument advanced at page 11, viz: "the cxp< rience and capability men from bring with tliem '' Controller situations are the mother-eoun ry would generally 6 lied in Deumaik by individuals Irom tue army, and, what peculiar qualifications are they expected to bring to the new poet r Certain. y no other than honesty and attention, and, we believe these are ot native growth, as abundantly found as in the mother country The

most Useful acquit eiueuts for a custom's contiollor, are a ennui knowledge of goods or merchandize, their sundry qualities and prices, method of packing, contents of packages and pieces &e and, as ninny articles are imported here, which are never seen in Detimatk, it is quite evident that a persou newly arrived here aud placed iu our Custom House, would find himself just as much a stranger in Ins ik w situation, as wheu he originally entered the business in the mother country. We believe it was first seen on Monday evening There can be no doubt that it is the same comet which came into view in Europe in the early part of the month of May, and to which we relerred in this paper ol the 17th of that month It has a very long tail, and reminds one of the comet of 1843; hut this one, il we can credit the calculations of astronomers in reference to these erratic bodies, will appear in þÿ1865 its period of revolution being supposed to be 2ljj years. In a scientific article which we rend some time ago on solar spots, it. is supposed by the writer that these spots are the impure portions of the sun which, from time to time, ate required to be thrown off, and that the visits of comets to the neighbourhood of the suit resulted to gathering up these impurities; for, says the writer, "it is not opposed to observed facts, to find that the spots have disippeared after the visit of a comet." It is curious, in connection with this supposition to find that during the last month, as stated by Major Lang in a letter to us, there were several large spots visible on the sun's dise; and that there is at present visible a latge, black, circular, spot which can be seen with a cotnmou spy glass Should this supposition obtaiu auy credi1 among astronomers, it would add a little to the interest taken iu the visits of these dustmen ol the solar system.

(From the ST. Thomas Times. July 6th, 1861.) In a recent sitting of the Colonial Council we find His Excellency the Governor exposing himself in the following language: þÿ has It generally been the case that a rather considerable amount of the customs revenue In St. Thomas have been required to cover the deficit, which the expenditure in St. Croix over and above the revenue would otherwise have caused, and there was iu bis opinion nothing wrong in principle in allowing this to continue, even after a separation of the finances of the Colonies from those of the Mother-country, as the revenne deriv" cd from the customs in 8t. Thomas, where they were essentially a transit duty which did not, as the duty in St. Croix fall on the inhabitants, but were paid on goods that were in transitn to foreign countries, must be considered as a general revenue to tho state, and of a different nature to the general taxes, the surplus of which the State might very well dispose of for the benefit of tb« Colonies in general and not for any island in particular. It had been his opinion that if a separation of the finances of the Colonies from those of the Mother-country was to take place, a ( point to gain which he thought desirable, and which he intended to prepare the way for, it would be the most desirable to main- I tain a common budget for the three islands, and not divide St. Croix from St. Thomas." As the foregoing is of much moment to St Thomas, it would be unreasonable to expect her to keep silent in the matter. His Excel-

lency maintains that as the Customs revenues here are derived from goods þÿ tn þÿtransitu, those revenues cannot properly be held as coming or accruing from the inhabitants, and for that reason the Island may not have any claim to the benefits arising there! ruu>; at least sncli is the maunor in which we comprehend His Excellency. The Spanish proverb might here be very properly applied However, in order that we may be understoood, we shall endeavour to cite a parallel or two, adapted, as we believe, to our case The Isthmus of Panama is destined to become the great highway between the East and West. On the acquisition of California by the Americans, a shoit road thereto became most desirable for the purpose of trado, and a Railroad across the aforesaid Isthmus was at once projected by the capitalists of New York, and a eompauy accordingly formed There may be many, the shareholders exoepted, Dot acquainted with the concessions that company had

s T« s m i i # y is. to make to the Republic of New Granada before they secured transitu þÿ along that narrow nerkol land. H ie 1 are a few of the concessions: The carrying of New Granadian troops free of chajge uu tin: ' line; the conveyance ol all New Granadian mail matter free of ehage; an annual contribution ' for the right of way þÿ we disreincmber the -urn; and at tlie expiration of forty five years the Railroad to revert to the GoVei ninent of Now Gianada The Isthmus derives all those benefits to whieh may tie added that Panama is rapidly becoming a regenerated city, and another, (Aspinwail,) is spi inging up with magic effect on the Atlantic side. And would it have been right that all these advantages should have heeo I Islands, in case the finances ol the Colonies should ignored to the country itself, simply because the foreign pa senger-, mails, specie and inerchandi-e were only þÿ in þÿtransitu, ? England, after al , is only a country whose tiade is þÿ in the one published in the þÿ transitu','' nearly all the produce bought by her on this continent, one writ read by the charter parti s, is shipped for Falmouth or Queenstown, for orders. What does this imply ? That if the continental mark os are favorable the produce will go forward, if not, it will go to oDu of | force on a population, who either directly or the principal sea-ports of tiie kingdom, and there landed and stored to await a change of trade. Would England he content to lose the advantages winch such trade produces, because some

oue should say it was ouly þÿ in transitu," and more especially when it is the capital of her merchants that creates it? In t lie same way it I he both comical and injurious to foice on a is the capital of the merchant of Si. Thomas that causes these goods to tome here, not þÿ in show themselves unwilling to receive that rigln; þÿtransitu but when received, duly unpacked aud displayed out, to meet the wants and tastes of bis expected customers Irom ahioad, aud if it should be his misfortune to misjudge those wants and tastes the goods become dead stock, and his transactions, at tho close of tile year, are by no means encouraging. Therefore, if it is the geuerous disposition of the mother country not to claim any surplus revenues from the colonies, hut simply desiring them to he self-sustaining, it is but ju.-t at.d reasonable that whatever we may have over in our public receipts should he held for the purpose of executing those public works, so much needed to perpetuate that self same trade and commerce, aud which, if long delayed, others over watchful of sur condition, will not fail to take due advantage of. It is further staled in the Council that the main cause of the heavy expenditure iu St. Croix is owing to her having so large a military establishment; if such is the case wo would, with a somewhat interested motive, wo confess, imp ure our neighboui8 of St. Croix, to iuculcate the habits of brotherly love, a good Christian sentiment, and the principles of peace and good order,

so as there may be uo need of their having soldiers, and thereby relieve us of the burden of paying for them. We have before this expressed ourself in this paper that St. Thomas is the þÿ goose that lays tire golden þÿegg, aud, according to tire theory we are now humbly cn leavouting to combat, it would appear that she is to be for all time retained as the auriferous goo-.e ! Wo thank the honorable first member for Gbristiaustcd, on behalf ot the public lreie, for his advocating that each Island should he allowed to have a separate budget. If this is not conceded, there is very little hope that St. Tin mas will ever be enabled to effect those improvements, which evciy one intimately acquainted with her condition, kuows she so much requires.

Ouk columns have for some time been occupied with a correspondence relating to the affairs of St. Jo þÿn s Chur, li, which, though necessary perhaps, has still been painful to a portion of our readers. We say painful, because it is a subject of regret, that where harmony and peace prevailed so long under the rectorship of former ministers, the contrary qualities | should now unfortunately have usurped their place. This unfortunate state has evidently beeu maintained through that want of unanimity so dangerously prevalent in all classes of this community. Before we close, we must beg leave to make a few remarks to the small remnant of the Vestry now existing, and which we hope will be taken in good part, as our intention in interfering in this matter is not for the purpose of making the existing breach wider, but only, if possible, to endeavour to heal those differences so unhappily existing. COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the St Croix Avis, Sir, As a tribute of respect and gratitude to the Reverend Edwin O. Roach, rector of All Saiuts' Church St. Thomas, who is now among us on a visit, aud officiating as minister in St John's Church, the prtseut is intended, while I also beg to be peimittcd to make a lew other observations, in reference to Mr. Almou. The rector of St. John's Church, Mr. Alinon, after deeply sowiug the seed of di.content in the congregation of said church; after being the means of creating dissensious aud enmity am.ODg families and among friends ; after trying to abolish old established cus oms in the church nnd the rules by which a church, guided by the rules of the church of England, is sustained ; after iutroducing an absurd novelty whereby the industry of the rural population is lik ly to he endangered and encouraging the preaching of Moravians in our Sabbath school room, betakes himself to St Thomas on a visit, to officiate as minister in All Saints' Parish there during Mr. Roach's 8' journ among its. It was at first supposed here by the orthodox christians of St. John's parish that the object of Mr. Roach's visit, was to try and reconcile the differences that existed in the parish, and the chu eh was c pccially much crowded on the first Sunday, that he should hold divine service; each one to hear and judge for himself whether this worthy gentleman would sink himself in the estimation of the proper thinking portion of the congregation (and community) by at-

tempting to support the conduct of the lector, not only contrary to the established customs of this place, but contrary to the belief of all the orthodox christians of the Church of England' But we were all pleasingly disappointed by his not making the slightest reference to the matter!!! Then, for the first time in nine or ten months, we felt as if wc were worshipping our Creator, according as we bad been taught in childhood to do, free of any foreign religious principles, and, although we do not condemn any oilier sect (whether Moravian or Methodist) for the manner in which they have been early taught to worship their Maker, wo would decidedly object to having Moravian principles of religion, introduced into our Church of England faith. The Reverend E. Roach appears to he hut too sensible of the necessity of keeping into the fraternity, by not having countenanced by his presence the meeting on Monday evening last iu St. John's Sunday school room, where only Mr. Gotz (a Moravian) officiated, and, had this gentleman exercised his proper j"dgmeut, ho would havo seen the presumption of his holding sucli a meeting in the school room of St John's Church, wheu the officiating minister discountenanced same, by not deigning to give even his preseuce. Pray, Mr. Editor why did not Mr. Goiz hold the meeting in his own church and why should not these meetings always he held

._ in the Moravian Church, being a place perhaps more suited to such kind of lecturing or, as, some term it, revivalism. Wo could certainly then not object to Air. Almou's visiting the Moravian Church, if ho felt inclined to lecture at buclt meetings, provided his proper duties did not require him at his own, but we most decidedly object to, and put our faces against any act or acts, whereby the probability of any foreign religions principles, are likely to bo introduced here iu St. John's Church. I have myself had a short conversation with the Reverend Roach, aud although we did not enter in detail into the present religious differences in St. John's Church, his conversation proved to me, that his opinions (independent of Ins openly acting widely different iu many rerpects from Mr. Almon's religious principles)

During the few days he has been among us ho preceded two corpses atluuerals (both parlies being attached to the church of England) being present at the house of mourning uir both occasions, and I know he declared to a ccrtaiu individual, that he found it a pleasure iu the di charge of his sacred religious duties, to havo ths opportunity of offering a word of c insolation, to the family aud friends of a deceased. For a miuister to precede a corpse at funerals here, is one of the many long established customs ol this island, aud this is another of the customs, which I notice Mr. Ahnon refuses to comply with. A great many of us will regret when this worthy minister leaves us for his own pa isli and, although. we do not envy the congregation of All Saint's Church so kind a minister (being able now to realize why he is so highly esteemed by them) we feel nevertheless despondent at parting with the Reverend Roach, to be again replaced by the rector Mr. Almon, with whom tho orthodox chiisiiaus of that church are to justly dissatisfied. I am, dear Sir, Your Olidt. Scrvt. An Episcopalian. St. Croix, 21st September 1861.

The 3rd orown-member (Stakemann) regretted the evident necessity for the division of tho Colonial Council, owing to the continued ah fence of members from St. Thomas. The passing of the present Draft he considered impracticable. The Ministry would, as a matter of course, wish to hear the opinion of the inhabitants of St. Thomas before taking any 6tcps in tho matter. Ho should vote against tbe draft ; the moro so, as it was closely connected with other drafts that he would vote against.

The 5th member for Christianstcd (Rothe) likewise regretted the absence of members for St. Thomas. He objected to the present draft' If the representatives of the Colonies were to be entrusted with legislative power, it ought to be in a different form from that proposed in the present draft. It would be likewise much bettor to postpone the question of a separation of the Council until the question of the amount of legislative power to bo entrusted to the oolonial representative assemblies was decided. The 1st member for Frederiksted fSarauw) begged the Council to remember, that the inhabitants af St. Thomas wished for a separation. What was produced iu the present draft was only, what the Colonial Law had suggested. add, that, in deciding the question of a division of the Colonial Council, agreeably to the 1st of the Colonial Law, it could not bo overlooked that the present proposal had been brought forward in immediate connection with another proposal for a separation of the taxation of tho island of St. Croix from the finances of the mothorcountry, and for coDoeding to the Colonial Council of that island legislative power. When tho 1st of the Colonial Law was framed, it had not been pre-supposed that cither of the separate Colonial Councils was to have any such new power. If the constitutional institutions in such of the British Westiudia Colonies that possessed legislative assemblies were to be cited as examples, it would be found that tho legislative power was, perhaps with a single exception, never entrusted to one assembly, tut that there existed a Legislative Council, the members of which were elected by the Crown, besides tho representative Assembly, pioperly so called. The present draft, in its immediate connection with tho other draft mentioned that had been introduced by the same members, aimed, on the contrary, at transferring to a separate Council for St. Croix, to consist of 10 members, a legislative power in questions of the greatest importance ; and this he must declare to be entirely unadvisable. From the London Times, August 20. St. Domingo. þÿ Some official despatches have been published relating to the annexation of Eastern Santo Domingo to Spain. The proclamation of annexation was made in the Square in the presenceof less than 300 regular troops and National Guards, and, of about 250 people, of whom at least 200 were Spaniards, and other foreigners. Troops were forthwith sent from Cuba and Porto Rico to protect the country against any attack from the Ilaytians. There are many persons in St. Domingo who were slaves in Cuba or Porto Rico and effected their escape years ago, and some of them have risen to high rank in the army ; and upon our Consul inquiring of the diplomatic secretary of the Commander-in-Chicf of the Spanish expedition to St. lJomingo what effect the present change would have upon them, that functionary replied that their owners would have a perfect right to claim them as slaves, and the Spanish Government could not refuse to give them up. The same principle might he made to apply to all who became free when the Spanish part of the island declared itself independent in 1821, and to their children. But upon Lord J. Russell causing inquiry to be made at Madrid, Marshal þÿO Donnell gave the strongest assurances that the freedom of these persons would be in no wise interfered with, and that now henceforward slaves, under whatever denomination they arrived at St. Domingo, whether with or without their owners, would be entitled to their freedom as much as if they landed

on the peninsula of Spain ; and Senor Collantes stated, that the Spanish Government, þÿ having resolved not to re-establish slavery, will always consider all the inhabitants of colour residing in St. Domingo as þÿfree. The preamble of the Royal decree of re-incorporation states, þÿ þÿ < The inhabitants are free. Slavery, which is a necessity in other provinces, is not requisite for the cultivation of that fertile soil, re-establish þÿit. Lord J. Russell si and your þÿMajesty s Government will not ed a decree to that effect, but the Sp.i Minister for Foreign Affairs replied th u would require a special law for the purpose before slavery could he established in St. Domingo, and in the present age ol civilization and, above all, taking into consideration the sentiments of the Spanish people, no Ministry could bring forward and no Cortes pass such a law. His Excellency further said, þÿ that the public feeling in Spain was against the slave trade, and the Spanish Government was using its best endeavours to put a stop to it, but that its total suppression could not he effected in a day, or before measures for substituting other labour were maþÿtured. In a despatch of the 14th of May Lord J. Russell counsels the Spanish Government to consider, that when the civil war in America shall be brought to an end, both the North and the South may combine to make the occupation of the Dominican territory by Spain the cause of serious differences, and that as þÿ it is a fundamental maxim of British policy to

wish well to Spain, any combination of events which might involve the possibility of Spain being engaged in a conflict which, from local circumstances and disadvantages, might be in the end seriously injuriously to her rule over her ancient possessions, would he viewed by Her þÿMajesty s Government with lively apprehension and sincere þÿregret. þÿ þÿ The Loss oe the Asiatic. þÿ The sad details of the foundering of the Asialic, a ship of nearly 1,000 þÿtons burden, while on her homeward voyage from Akyab to Falmouth (for orders), and the loss of the greater portion of her officers and crew, were made known yesterday at þÿLloyd s by the receipt of despatch þÿa from þÿLloyd agent s at St. Helena. The survivors, nine in number, had reached that island by the Hanoverian hark Olympia, Captain Tobias, which picked them up on the morning after the loss of their ship. Among the survivors is Captain Watts, the commander of the Asiatic, who gives Ihe following version of the sad catastrophe which befel his ship and so many of his crew. It appears that the Asiatic started on her voyage from Akyab on the 28th of March last. The weather was far from favourable, and continued boisterous till the 4th of June. On that day they encountered a heavy gale from the S.S.W., compelling them to hove the ship to under lower mainsail for 12 hours. Fine weather set in, which prevailed until the 15th of that month, when the weather again became had. The ship was then in lat. 34 56 S., long. 27 E. On the fol-

lowing day, the 16th, the weather returned fine, hut on the 17th a gale sprung up from the north-west of a most threatening character. They took in all sail, and hove to on the starboard tack under lower maintopsails. By 9 þÿo clockthe gale had increased to almost o hurricane, with a turbulent sea, which caused the ship to labour violently and ship large quantities of water, filling the decks fore and aft. About this time a sail could he observed some

four miles distant, evidently in the same seen to be trying position hove as the Asiatic She was to on the same tack, and was- under the main-trysail. 1 he Asiþÿatic spumps, never ceased working tor a moment. About noon a terrific sea caught the ship, washed away port bulwark, port quarter-boat, galley, water- cask, and everything on deck. At 5 30 p.m. another sea struck the ship, which drove in the front of the poop and topgallant-forecastle, and carried away all the internal fittings. The storm gradually became more furious and the ship rolled and laboured greater than before. The pumps although kept constantly going, could not relieve the ship o! much water. From this time up to midnight the gale continued to rage with increased violence. About half-past 2 on the following morning, the 18th, the ship was evidently last settling down, the foretopmast and topsail were set, with a view of wearing the vessel round; | and the helm had been put np, when, all of a sudden, the crew at the time being engaged hauling main brace, the in ship fell on on the her weather broadside and commenced sinking. her planks, and it was with the greatest difficulty and exertion At that prevent her sinking. times they could she was half-full of water, and they kept bailing her out with their boots and caps. With the exception ot one man, they saw nothing of the remainder of the crew. They endeavoured to save him, but, o win"' to the strong and heavy sea runniii",''they could not reach him. The survivors in the boat kept head to wind until daylight, using the bottom boards ir. the boat for paddles, having lost the oars. THE Hth MEETING of the Council was held on Saturday the 13th of July 1861. Absent were: the 3rd member for Fiederik sted (Castouier) and the 2nd member for St. Johns (Christmas). The minutes of the last meeting were read. The 1st question on the order of the day was the 2nd discussion of the þÿGovernment sdraft of a law containing modifications in the law of 30th June 1850, together with the draft of a law altering the same law, introduced by the 5 members of the committee appointed to report on the þÿGovernment draft. s The following amendment was proposed by His Excellency the Governor to tiro Governþÿment draft, s viz : that the following new be added : $ 3. On Sugar, Rum and Molasses, imported for consumption in St. Croix from St. Thomas and St. Johns, is to be deducted from the importduty in St. Croix, the amount of duty which by the clearance from either of the said two islands is proved to have been paid there, in the same manner as allowed by 9 of the law of 30th June 1850 with regard to the exportduties. The Governor remarked with regard to the proposed addition of a new to the Governþÿment Draft, s that the 1st member for St. Johns (Elliott) had some days ago privately complained, that when produce from St. Johns was imported to this island, without being intended for exportation, full import-duty of 12J per Ct. of the value was cxactod, although the Statetreasury bad already collected duty on the same produce in St. Johns. In consequence hereof he (the Governor) had obtained informa-

tion from the custom-houses in the island and had ascertained, that a different proceeding was observed in this respect at the different customhouses, for, at the custom house in Christiansted a reduction in the import-duty had been allowed for the amount of duty paid in St. Johns, namely 5 per Ct. on the value of sugar and cts. pr. Gallon of Rum, notwithstanding that the produce had been imported for consumption in the island; but at the custom-house in Frcderiksted, where such importations occurred oftencr than in Christiansted, a contrary proceeding was observed, as the reduction was only granted for the special case treated of in 9 of the Law of 30th June 1850, namely when the produce imported from St. Johns was again exported.
